characters: The Buddha (days 1-6, after his awakening): a man in his late 30s to 40s in the style of respectful traditional Buddhist painting, calm oval face with half-lowered eyes, elongated earlobes, short tight dark curls with the small rounded crown-knot (ushnisha), no beard, warm ochre-saffron robe draped over the left shoulder with the right shoulder bare, barefoot, carrying a dark alms bowl when walking, a soft subtle radiance around him (no harsh halo). The seeker Siddhattha before awakening (day 5): the same face, very thin after six years of fasting, short dark hair (no crown-knot), a worn faded ochre cloth. The Bharadvaja brahmin (day 1): about 50, gray-streaked black hair tied in a top-knot, short gray beard, white cotton dhoti and shawl, sacred thread across the chest, sandals. Never Disparaging (day 2): a monk about 40, shaved head, gentle round face, patched faded brown-orange robe, barefoot, painted in East Asian Mahayana style. The bowl bearer (day 3): a young man about 25, short black hair, bare-chested with a plain cream lower cloth, intense focused eyes. The guard (day 3): broad man about 35, black mustache, red turban, leather vest, upright curved sword. The star performer (day 3): a dancer about 25 in a long, fully covering jeweled crimson-and-gold dance costume with bells at the ankles; shown only as spectacle, never romantic. The five ascetics (day 4): five gaunt men aged 30-50, long matted hair tied up, scraggly beards, bare torsos with simple ochre lower cloths; Kondanna is the eldest, gray-bearded. Sujata (day 5): a young woman about 20 from a village headman's family, long black braid, rose-pink and gold sari, gold bangles, modest and kind; her servant girl in plain blue. Dona (day 6): a brahmin about 45, shaved head with a small tuft, white dhoti and shawl, wooden walking staff. King Milinda (day 7): about 40, Indo-Greek look, short curly brown hair and trimmed beard, gold diadem, white and purple Greek-style robes with Indian jewelry. Nagasena (day 7): a monk about 35, shaved head, lean face, deep saffron robe, calm steady gaze. Modern families (each film's last picture) are new real-looking people each day, in casual current clothes.

1.story: The insulting brahmin and the uneaten food (Akkosa Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 7.2)
1.point: Karma means action and the intention inside it, so you own what you do and don't have to take on what others throw at you.
1.script: A man stormed up to the Buddha, furious. Someone from his own clan had just become a monk. So he shouted every insult he knew. The Buddha let him finish. Then he asked one question. When guests come to your house, do you offer them food? Yes. And if they don't eat it, whose food is it? Mine, the man said. So it is with your insults, said the Buddha. I don't accept them. They stay with you. That's karma. Not the universe paying people back. Karma means action, and the Buddha said the intention inside it is what counts. Your choices shape you. When someone comes at you online, their words are theirs. What you do next is yours.

2.story: Never Disparaging Bodhisattva (Lotus Sutra, chapter 20), leading into the three bows to the three jewels
2.point: Buddhists bow three times to the three jewels: the Buddha (a person who woke up), the Dharma (his teaching) and the Sangha (the community), not to a statue.
2.script: A monk named Never Disparaging had one practice. He bowed to every person he met. Rich, poor, strangers, rude ones. And he told each one: I would never look down on you. You can become a buddha too. People found it strange. Some got angry. They threw sticks and stones at him. He stepped back, out of reach, and bowed again, from a distance. That's from the Lotus Sutra. When Buddhists bow three times, it isn't to a statue. One bow to the Buddha, a person who woke up. One to the Dharma, his teaching. One to the Sangha, the people who walk it together. The three jewels. Bow to what can wake up in anyone. Even the kid who's rude to you.

3.story: The bowl of oil through the crowd (Janapadakalyani Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 47.20)
3.point: Sati, the old word behind 'mindfulness', means remembering to notice: holding your attention steady while everything pulls it away.
3.script: A huge crowd packed the town square. The most famous star in the land was singing and dancing, and everyone was screaming. Then a man was handed a bowl, filled to the brim with oil. His task: carry it right between the crowd and the stage. Behind him walked a guard with a raised sword. Spill one drop, and that's the end of you. Would he look up at the show? Not once. The Buddha told this story, and then said: the bowl is mindfulness. The old word is sati. It's related to a word for memory. Not just paying attention. Remembering to, step after step, while everything screams at you to look away. Your phone buzzes all day. Sati is remembering your bowl.

4.story: The first sermon to the five companions at the deer park near Varanasi (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, SN 56.11; the five's snub from Vinaya Mahavagga I.6 / Majjhima Nikaya 26); doctor comparison from later teachers (Visuddhimagga XVI)
4.point: The four noble truths are a diagnosis, not a verdict: there is dukkha, it has a cause (craving), it can end, and there's a path.
4.script: Five monks had given up on their old friend. He'd quit their starving practice, so they called him soft. When he walked into the deer park near Varanasi, they agreed: don't stand, don't greet him. But as he came closer, they couldn't help it. One took his bowl. One brought water. And he told them what he'd found. One: there is dukkha, the ache of loss and change. Two: it has a cause, craving, wanting things other than they are. Three: it can end. Four: there's an eight-part path. The four noble truths. Later teachers compared it to a doctor's visit. Not a verdict that life is bad. A diagnosis, and a cure. Hard week? It's not just you. It's not the end.

5.story: Sujata's offering of milk rice before the awakening (Nidanakatha, the Jataka commentary) and the morning alms round; the Buddha's line on the fruit of giving (Itivuttaka 26)
5.point: Dana means giving: it fills the monks' alms bowls, it is a practice for the giver, and in the Buddha's teaching it comes first.
5.script: A seeker had starved himself for six years, trying to break through. He was skin and bone, sitting under a tree. A young woman named Sujata came with a golden bowl of milk rice, an offering she'd promised. She gave it to him. He ate. His strength came back. And that very night, sitting beneath another tree, he woke up. He became the Buddha. It began with a gift. That's dana: giving. Giving still fills Buddhist monks' bowls today. At dawn they walk with covered bowls. They don't ask. People give, and often the givers bow. Not begging: an exchange. The Buddha said, if people knew the fruit of giving, they'd never eat without sharing. Give first. Your lunch, your time, a hand.

6.story: Dona and the footprints, 'remember me as awake' (Dona Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 4.36), leading into Vesak
6.point: Buddha is a title meaning 'one who woke up', and on Vesak many Buddhists celebrate his birth, awakening and death on one spring full moon.
6.script: A priest named Dona saw footprints on a road. Not ordinary ones. Each held the mark of a wheel, with a thousand spokes. He followed them to a tree, where a man sat, calm and bright. Dona asked: are you a god? No. A heavenly spirit? No. A human being? No. Then what are you? Remember me, he said, as awake. In the old language: buddha. It's not a name. It's a title. One who woke up. That's who Buddhists celebrate on Vesak, a full moon in spring. In many lands it marks his birth, his awakening and his death, all at once. Lanterns everywhere. Not for a god. For a person who woke up. So waking up is something people do.

7.story: King Milinda and the monk Nagasena: the lamp burning through the night (Milindapanha II.2.1) and the lamp lit from a lamp (Milindapanha III.5.5)
7.point: Buddhist rebirth isn't a soul moving into a new body; like a flame lit from a flame, what carries on is neither the same nor someone else.
7.script: King Milinda loved to win arguments, so he put a hard one to a monk named Nagasena. When someone is reborn, is it the same person, or someone else? Neither, said the monk. Picture a lamp burning all night. Is the flame at midnight the same flame from the evening? No. Is it a different lamp, then? Also no. It's one lamp, flame lit from flame. Rebirth is like that. Many Buddhist traditions teach that one life is followed by another, shaped by karma. But no soul packs up and moves. What carries on is momentum, like one flame lighting the next. Even now, each moment is lit from the last. Who you were last year isn't who you are now. But it lit you.

sources_check: Day 1: Akkosa Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 7.2) for the story; Nibbedhika Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 6.63) for 'intention is kamma'; Upajjhatthana Sutta (AN 5.57) for 'owner of my actions'
Day 2: Lotus Sutra ch. 20 (Sadaparibhuta / Never Disparaging Bodhisattva); Khuddakapatha 1 (the three refuges)
Day 3: Janapadakalyani Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 47.20), the bowl of oil; sati related to Sanskrit smrti (memory)

Day 4: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11); the five's agreement to snub him and then serving him: Vinaya Mahavagga I.6 / Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26); doctor comparison: Visuddhimagga XVI
Day 5: Nidanakatha (Jataka commentary) for Sujata's milk rice; Itivuttaka 26 for 'if beings knew the fruit of giving and sharing they would not eat without giving'; Theravada alms round practice
Day 6: Dona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 4.36); Vesak as the triple commemoration in Theravada lands
Day 7: Milindapanha II.2.1 (lamp burning through the watches of the night, neither the same nor another) and III.5.5 (lamp lit from a lamp)
risks: Day 1: The sutta says the brahmin was angry that a brahmin of his Bharadvaja clan went forth under the Buddha; the script says 'someone from his own clan'. The food simile and 'they stay with you' are a close paraphrase, not a quote.

Day 2: Never Disparaging's words paraphrase the Lotus Sutra ('I deeply respect you... you will all become buddhas'); 'you can become a buddha too' simplifies the Mahayana teaching. It is a Mahayana story used to explain a bow shared across schools; check Theravada viewers are comfortable with it.

Day 3: The sutta's figure is the janapadakalyani, 'the most beautiful girl of the land', singing and dancing; the script and pictures render her as 'the most famous star' to avoid any romance angle. The sword-bearer's threat is in the sutta but toned down ('that's the end of you'). 'Related to a word for memory' is the soft version of sati/smrti sharing a root.

Day 4: The doctor comparison is credited to 'later teachers' (Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga), not to the Buddha; the eight parts of the path are mentioned but not named. Who took the bowl and brought water follows the Vinaya account loosely.

Day 5: Sujata's story is from the Jataka commentary (later tradition, not the early suttas); 'a golden bowl', 'six years' and 'that very night' follow that tradition. 'It began with a gift' is our framing. The Itivuttaka 26 line is paraphrased. Picture 1 shows the Buddha-to-be very thin: keep it respectful, not grotesque.

Day 6: In the Dona Sutta the Buddha's 'no' to 'human being' means the taints that would make him a god or a human are abandoned; a scholar should confirm the short version doesn't sound like he denies being a person, since the film then calls him 'a person who woke up' (matching the lesson). Vesak as a triple commemoration is Theravada; the narration says 'in many lands' to stay open to East Asian practice.

Day 7: Milinda is traditionally identified with the Indo-Greek king Menander; the palace picture uses Indo-Greek styling. The script blends two lamp similes (II.2.1 and III.5.5). Picture 6 assumes a Tibetan 49-day practice with a butter lamp and khata; check the details.
All days: the Buddha is shown, as the brief allows; check each painting follows respectful traditional iconography (no casual or comic poses, feet not pointed at the viewer).
